families.name: Analysis, architecture & leadership
families.intro: These are the jobs that decide what gets built, how it fits together and who builds it, rather than writing most of the code themselves. The family starts with analysts and data processing managers translating business paperwork into machine jobs, then branches into architecture, product and people management, and finally reaches the boardroom as CIO and CTO.

families.name: Networks & security
families.intro: These jobs keep machines talking to each other and keep the wrong people out of the conversation. The line runs from telephone exchanges to office LANs, then to the internet and the cloud, and the security branch grew alongside it, moving from policy and audit to hands-on breaking, building and, most recently, probing AI models.

families.name: Data & AI
families.intro: These jobs are about turning recorded facts into answers, and later into products that learn. The family starts with statisticians and the keepers of tapes and databases, grows through warehouses and pipelines into data science, and in its newest branch builds software around large AI models.

families.name: Operations & infrastructure
families.intro: These are the people who keep software running once it leaves a developer's hands: the machines, the deployments, the alarms at 3 a.m. The family starts with operators feeding tapes and printouts to a single mainframe, passes through administrators who hand-tended fleets of servers, and ends with engineers who treat infrastructure as code and sell it to colleagues as an internal product.

families.name: Quality & test
families.intro: Quality and test is the family that asks whether the software actually works. It began as people running programs by hand and logging what broke, then steadily became a coding job of its own, until much of the testing is itself software running inside the build pipeline.

families.name: Development
families.intro: Development covers the people who turn intent into working instructions for a machine. It starts with human calculators and hand coders, consolidates around the Programmer, then fans out by layer (systems, applications, web, mobile, embedded) and by seniority, as the work moved from a clerical task to an engineering discipline with its own career ladder.

families.name: Support & customer-facing
families.intro: These jobs face the people who buy, use or are stuck with technology: installing it, explaining it, selling it and fixing it when it breaks. The family begins with engineers who serviced machines on customer sites and splits into a support ladder and a technical sales ladder, which meet again in hybrid roles embedded with customers.

nodes.title: Systems Analyst
nodes.what: Studies how a business process works today, then specifies what a computer system should do to replace or improve it. The job sits between the people with the problem and the programmers, producing requirements, data flows and procedure designs.
nodes.roots: A root of the family that seeded several later titles: Business Analyst grew from it, Analyst/Programmer merged it with coding, and it shaped the Solutions Architect role.

nodes.title: Data Processing (DP) Manager
nodes.what: Ran the data processing department: the machine room, its operators, programmers and punched-card workflow. Scheduling batch runs, budgeting for expensive hardware and keeping payroll and billing jobs on time were the core of the work.
nodes.roots: A root title from the mainframe era; as computing spread beyond a single back-office department, the role grew into the broader IT Manager.

nodes.title: Project Manager (software)
nodes.what: Owns the plan for delivering a software project: scope, schedule, budget, risks and status reporting. Unlike a technical lead, the focus is coordination and commitments rather than design decisions or code.
nodes.roots: A root borrowed from engineering and defense project practice; it later grew into the Scrum Master / Agile Coach and influenced the rise of the Product Manager.

nodes.title: Technical Lead / Lead Programmer
nodes.what: A senior hands-on developer who sets the technical direction for a team, reviews designs and code, and unblocks others while still shipping features. Authority comes from expertise, not from managing people.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Programmer / Computer Programmer as teams got bigger and someone had to own the design; it later grew into Engineering Manager.

nodes.title: CIO
nodes.what: The executive accountable for an organization's internal information systems, from core business applications to infrastructure and IT spending. A CIO talks budgets, risk and business alignment with the rest of the leadership team.
nodes.roots: Grew out of IT Manager once information systems became a strategic asset worth a seat at the executive table; it also shaped how the CTO role was defined.

nodes.title: IT Manager
nodes.what: Manages the people and systems that keep an organization's computers, networks and business software running, from purchasing and vendor contracts to support staff and security basics.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Data Processing (DP) Manager as personal computers and networks spread through the office; at the top of the ladder it grew into the CIO.

nodes.title: CTO
nodes.what: Leads technology strategy, usually for a company whose product is technology. A CTO may be the top architect, the head of engineering, or an external-facing technical voice, depending on the company's size and needs.
nodes.roots: Shaped by two neighbors: the CIO model of a technology executive, and VP Engineering, which often feeds it or splits the work of running engineering with it.

nodes.title: Business Analyst
nodes.what: Gathers and clarifies what the business needs, writes requirements and user stories, and checks that what gets built actually solves the problem. The emphasis is on processes and stakeholders, not system internals.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Systems Analyst, keeping the requirements and stakeholder half of that job while design and technical specification moved to architects and developers.

nodes.title: Product Manager
nodes.what: Decides what a product should do and why, by talking to customers, weighing priorities and setting the roadmap. Product managers own outcomes such as adoption and revenue, while engineers own how features are built.
nodes.roots: Influenced by Project Manager (software), but focused on the product's direction rather than delivery schedules; it later grew into Platform Product Manager.

nodes.title: Software Architect
nodes.what: Designs the high-level structure of a software system: its components, interfaces, technology choices and the tradeoffs between them. The architect keeps the design coherent as many developers work on it.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Engineer as systems became too large for one person's head; it then grew into Solutions Architect.

nodes.title: Enterprise Architect
nodes.what: Looks across all of an organization's systems at once, setting standards, mapping capabilities and steering which platforms to keep, merge or retire. The time horizon is years, and the audience is often leadership.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Solutions Architect, widening the view from one project's solution to the entire portfolio of systems an organization runs.

nodes.title: Solutions Architect
nodes.what: Designs a specific technical solution to a specific business problem, often combining existing products, vendors and integrations. Many solutions architects work close to customers, sketching designs during sales or implementation.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Architect and was influenced by Systems Analyst; it then grew into both Enterprise Architect and Cloud Architect.

nodes.title: VP Engineering
nodes.what: Runs the engineering organization: hiring, structure, delivery, process and the managers who lead teams. Where a CTO may focus on technical vision, a VP Engineering focuses on execution and the health of the organization.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Engineering Manager as companies needed a manager of managers; it often influences or feeds into the CTO role.

nodes.title: Scrum Master / Agile Coach
nodes.what: Facilitates an agile team's rituals, removes obstacles and coaches the team and organization on working iteratively. The role has influence but deliberately little formal authority over the work itself.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Project Manager (software) as agile methods replaced up-front plans with short iterations and self-organizing teams.

nodes.title: Engineering Manager
nodes.what: Manages a team of software engineers: one-on-ones, hiring, career growth, staffing and keeping delivery on track. Many still review designs, but people and team health come before personal coding output.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Technical Lead / Lead Programmer as companies separated the people-management track from the technical track; it led on to VP Engineering.

nodes.title: Cloud Architect
nodes.what: Designs systems to run on public cloud services, choosing managed offerings, network layouts, security controls and cost models. The job blends application architecture with infrastructure decisions once made by operations teams.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Solutions Architect as cloud platforms made infrastructure something you design in code and configuration rather than buy and install.

nodes.title: Platform Product Manager
nodes.what: A product manager whose customers are internal engineers or external developers, deciding what an internal platform, API or developer tool should offer and measuring whether teams actually adopt it.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Product Manager and was influenced by Platform Engineer, as internal platforms started being treated as products with their own roadmaps.

nodes.title: Telecoms Engineer
nodes.what: Designs, installs and maintains the circuits, exchanges, radio links and cables that carry voice and signals over distance. The work is physical and electrical, about lines and switching rather than software on computers.
nodes.roots: A root of the family, older than computing itself; its know-how about lines and switching fed directly into the Network Administrator role once computers needed connecting.

nodes.title: Information Security Officer
nodes.what: Writes and enforces the rules about who may see which data, runs access reviews and audits, and answers to management when something leaks. Mostly policy, risk and compliance rather than technical hands-on work.
nodes.roots: A root of the security branch, created as shared computers began holding sensitive records; it later split into the hands-on Security Analyst and the executive CISO.

nodes.title: Network Administrator
nodes.what: Keeps an organization's local network running day to day: adding users and devices, managing switches, cabling, file and print sharing, and chasing down why a floor has lost connectivity.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Telecoms Engineer's line and switching skills and from the Systems Administrator, as office PCs and LANs made the network something that needed its own caretaker.

nodes.title: Security Analyst
nodes.what: Watches logs and alerts, investigates suspicious activity, assesses vulnerabilities and writes up incidents. Sits between the policy maker and the engineer, turning raw signals into a judgement about whether something is actually wrong.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Information Security Officer as networked systems produced more events than a policy role could review, creating demand for dedicated technical investigators.

nodes.title: Network Engineer
nodes.what: Designs and builds networks rather than just operating them: routing, switching, WAN links, firewalls and capacity planning. Configures routers by hand and decides how traffic should flow between sites and the internet.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Network Administrator as internet connectivity and multi-site networks demanded design skill, and it went on to spawn Network Architect, Cloud Network Engineer and to influence Security Engineer.

nodes.title: Network Architect
nodes.what: Sets the long-range shape of an organization's network: topology, standards, vendors and how it will grow. Spends more time on diagrams, reviews and trade-offs than on configuring individual devices.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Network Engineer as networks became large enough that someone senior had to own the overall design rather than individual changes.

nodes.title: Security Engineer
nodes.what: Builds and runs the defenses: firewalls, intrusion detection, identity systems, encryption and hardening standards. Where an analyst investigates, this role engineers the controls that make attacks harder in the first place.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Security Analyst, with strong influence from the Network Engineer, as internet-facing systems made security a matter of building infrastructure rather than reviewing it.

nodes.title: CISO
nodes.what: The executive who owns an organization's security risk: setting strategy and budget, reporting to the board, managing the security team and leading the response when a breach happens.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Information Security Officer when security became a board-level concern, with the first widely cited appointment at Citicorp in 1995.

nodes.title: Penetration Tester
nodes.what: Is paid to break in, with permission. Probes networks, applications and sometimes buildings or people for weaknesses, then writes a report showing how far an attacker could get and how to fix it.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Security Engineer as organizations wanted proof of their defenses from the attacker's side, and it later led to the AI Red Teamer.

nodes.title: Application Security Engineer
nodes.what: Focuses on the code rather than the network: threat modeling designs, reviewing source, running scanners and helping developers fix injection flaws, broken authentication and similar bugs before release.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Security Engineer as web applications became the main way in for attackers, needing specialists who could read and reason about software.

nodes.title: DevSecOps Engineer
nodes.what: Builds security checks into the delivery pipeline: dependency scanning, secrets detection, policy as code and hardened container images. Aims to make the secure path the automatic one so teams can ship quickly without a manual gate.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Application Security Engineer and the DevOps Engineer when continuous delivery made periodic manual security reviews too slow to keep up.

nodes.title: Cloud Network Engineer
nodes.what: Designs and runs networking inside cloud platforms: virtual networks, subnets, peering, load balancers, private links and hybrid connections back to on-premises sites, usually defined in code rather than on physical boxes.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Network Engineer, influenced by the Cloud Engineer, as workloads moved to the cloud and routing became software-defined configuration instead of hardware.

nodes.title: AI Red Teamer
nodes.what: Attacks AI models and the systems built on them, trying jailbreaks, prompt injection, data extraction and harmful-output tests. Reports failures so model builders can add safeguards before and after release.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Penetration Tester as large language models created a new attack surface where the target is a model's behavior rather than a server or application.

nodes.title: Statistician
nodes.what: Designs surveys and experiments, chooses the right models and tests, and draws careful conclusions from data while being honest about uncertainty. Rigor about sampling and inference is the core of the craft.
nodes.roots: A root of the family, far older than computers; it fed the Data Analyst and, together with that role, the Data Scientist.

nodes.title: Data / Tape Librarian
nodes.what: Catalogs, stores, retrieves and rotates the reels of magnetic tape and disk packs that hold an installation's data, making sure the right volume is mounted for each job and backups are kept safe.
nodes.roots: A root of the data branch from the mainframe era; its custody of stored data fed into the Database Administrator role once databases replaced loose files and tapes.

nodes.title: Database Administrator (DBA)
nodes.what: Installs, tunes, backs up and secures databases. Manages schemas, indexes, permissions and recovery, and is the person called when queries crawl or data must be restored after a failure.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Data / Tape Librarian and the Systems Programmer as database management systems arrived and needed a dedicated owner; it later led to the Data Warehouse / BI Developer.

nodes.title: Data Analyst
nodes.what: Pulls data with queries and spreadsheets, cleans it, and produces reports, dashboards and answers to concrete business questions. Less mathematical than a statistician, closer to day-to-day decisions.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Statistician as cheap PCs and databases put data within reach of businesses, and it went on to feed both Data Scientist and Analytics Engineer.

nodes.title: Data Warehouse / BI Developer
nodes.what: Builds the central reporting store an organization queries for history and trends: dimensional models, fact and dimension tables, and the reports and cubes that business users read.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Database Administrator as companies wanted to analyze data across systems without slowing their operational databases, and it led to the ETL Developer.

nodes.title: ETL Developer
nodes.what: Writes the extract, transform and load jobs that move data from source systems into the warehouse, often with dedicated ETL tools, handling schedules, data quality checks and late or broken feeds.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Data Warehouse / BI Developer as the loading side of warehousing became big enough to be its own specialty, later leading to Big Data / Hadoop Engineer and Data Engineer.

nodes.title: Data Scientist
nodes.what: Combines statistics, programming and domain knowledge to find patterns, build predictive models and run experiments, then explains the results to people who make decisions. Expected to code more than a statistician and model more than an analyst.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Statistician and the Data Analyst when web-scale data needed people who could both program and reason statistically; it led to Machine Learning Engineer and influenced Prompt Engineer.

nodes.title: Big Data / Hadoop Engineer
nodes.what: Runs and programs distributed clusters that store and process data too large for one machine, writing batch jobs across many nodes and keeping the cluster healthy.
nodes.roots: Grew from the ETL Developer as web companies outgrew traditional warehouses and adopted Hadoop-style distributed processing, and it led into the broader Data Engineer role.

nodes.title: Data Engineer
nodes.what: Builds and maintains the pipelines, storage and tooling that make data reliable and available for analysts, scientists and products. Treats data movement as software engineering, with code, tests and orchestration.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Big Data / Hadoop Engineer and the ETL Developer as the work broadened beyond one technology into general pipeline engineering, and it fed the Analytics Engineer.

nodes.title: Machine Learning Engineer
nodes.what: Takes models from notebooks into production: building training pipelines, serving models behind APIs, monitoring performance and retraining. More software engineer than researcher, focused on making models work reliably at scale.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Data Scientist, influenced by the Software Engineer, as companies needed models shipped and maintained; it later led to the AI Engineer and the MLOps Engineer.

nodes.title: Analytics Engineer
nodes.what: Transforms raw warehouse data into clean, tested, documented models that analysts can trust, usually in SQL with version control and software practices. Sits between pipeline building and business analysis.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Data Engineer and the Data Analyst once cloud warehouses made in-warehouse transformation cheap, leaving a gap between moving data and analyzing it.

nodes.title: Prompt Engineer
nodes.what: Writes, tests and refines the instructions and examples fed to large language models to get reliable outputs, building evaluation sets and comparing variants. Works through the model's input rather than by training it.
nodes.roots: Influenced by the Data Scientist's habit of experiment and evaluation, it arose when capable chat models appeared, and it soon folded into the AI Engineer role.

nodes.title: AI Engineer
nodes.what: Builds products on top of foundation models: wiring model APIs into applications, retrieval over company data, tool use, evaluations, and cost and latency trade-offs. Uses models more than trains them.
nodes.roots: Grew from the Machine Learning Engineer, the Software Engineer and the Prompt Engineer as building with hosted models became mostly an application engineering job, and it led to AI Agent / Context Engineer.

nodes.title: AI Agent / Context Engineer
nodes.what: Designs systems where models plan and act over many steps: choosing tools, managing memory and what goes into the context window, orchestrating sub-agents and evaluating whole task runs rather than single replies.
nodes.roots: Grew from the AI Engineer as models became capable enough to take multi-step actions, making context management and agent orchestration a specialty of its own.

nodes.title: Computer Operator
nodes.what: Ran the mainframe shift: mounting tapes and disk packs, loading card decks, starting batch jobs in the right order, watching the console for errors and collecting printouts. The machine was too expensive to sit idle, so the work never stopped.
nodes.roots: A root of the family; its hands-on console work led both to the Operations Analyst, who scheduled and monitored jobs, and to the Systems Administrator, who looked after whole systems.

nodes.title: Operations Analyst
nodes.what: Plans and monitors the production schedule: which batch jobs run when, what depends on what, and what to do when an overnight run fails. Less hands-on than an operator, more focused on procedures, runbooks and keeping service levels intact.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Computer Operator as job scheduling became complex enough to need dedicated planning, and its incident and runbook habits later fed into the Site Reliability Engineer.

nodes.title: Configuration Manager
nodes.what: Keeps track of exactly which versions of code, documents and components make up a given system or release, controls changes to them, and can reconstruct any past build. Common on large defense and government projects where traceability is mandatory.
nodes.roots: A root of the family, born from the discipline of controlling change on big engineering projects; it led to the Release Manager and the Build & Release Engineer.

nodes.title: Systems Administrator
nodes.what: Looks after a set of multi-user machines: creating accounts, applying patches, managing disks and backups, tuning performance and fixing whatever breaks. The generalist caretaker who knows where every config file lives and who last touched it.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Computer Operator and the Systems Programmer as minicomputers and shared systems needed someone to own them; it later branched into Unix, Windows, network and virtualization specialties.

nodes.title: Systems Engineer
nodes.what: Designs and builds server environments rather than just maintaining them: choosing hardware, standardizing operating system builds, planning capacity and integrating storage and networking. A sysadmin with a longer horizon and more say over architecture.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Systems Administrator as organizations wanted someone to engineer their server estate up front, and it evolved into the broader Infrastructure Engineer.

nodes.title: Unix / Linux Administrator
nodes.what: Runs Unix and later Linux servers, living in the shell: writing scripts to automate chores, managing services and permissions, reading logs and squeezing reliability out of long-running boxes. Scripting fluency is what sets it apart from other admins.
nodes.roots: Specialized from the Systems Administrator as Unix spread through universities and data centers; its automation habits made it a direct ancestor of both the Site Reliability Engineer and the DevOps Engineer.

nodes.title: Windows Administrator
nodes.what: Manages Windows servers and the corporate desktop estate around them: directory services, group policies, file shares, email servers and patch cycles. Works more through management consoles and vendor tooling than through shell scripts.
nodes.roots: Specialized from the Systems Administrator as Windows servers took over office networks, splitting the profession into Unix and Windows camps with different tools and cultures.

nodes.title: Release Manager
nodes.what: Coordinates getting a release out the door: agreeing what goes in, tracking readiness across teams, running go/no-go meetings and scheduling the deployment window. More about people, risk and calendars than about compiling code.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Configuration Manager as software releases became multi-team events that needed someone to own the plan, and it fed into the Build & Release Engineer.

nodes.title: Build & Release Engineer
nodes.what: Owns the machinery that turns source code into shippable artifacts: build scripts, version tagging, packaging, installers and the servers that run nightly builds. When the build is red, this is the person everyone looks at.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Configuration Manager and the Release Manager as building and packaging became a technical job of its own; it led directly to the DevOps Engineer and the CI/CD / Automation Engineer.

nodes.title: Site Reliability Engineer
nodes.what: Applies software engineering to running production: setting reliability targets, automating away repetitive operations work, carrying the pager and writing blameless postmortems. Distinct from classic ops in measuring risk explicitly and coding its way out of toil.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Unix / Linux Administrator and the Software Engineer, with influence from the Operations Analyst and Application Support Analyst; it later spawned the Chaos Engineer, Observability Engineer and Platform Engineer.

nodes.title: Infrastructure Engineer
nodes.what: Builds and runs the shared foundation that applications sit on: servers, storage, networks, load balancers and the provisioning tools that tie them together. A deliberately broad title that covers whatever layer sits beneath the product teams.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Systems Engineer as the job widened from individual servers to whole environments, and it fed into the Cloud Engineer once that foundation moved to rented platforms.

nodes.title: Virtualisation Engineer
nodes.what: Runs the hypervisor layer that carves physical servers into many virtual machines: building clusters, managing templates, migrating workloads and balancing capacity. Cut hardware sprawl and made server provisioning a matter of minutes rather than weeks.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Systems Administrator as hypervisors entered data centers, and its pooled, on-demand model of compute led straight to the Cloud Engineer.

nodes.title: DevOps Engineer
nodes.what: Bridges development and operations by automating the path from commit to production: pipelines, infrastructure as code, configuration management and monitoring. Ideally a culture of shared ownership; in practice often a title for whoever builds the tooling.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Build & Release Engineer and the Unix / Linux Administrator, influenced in both directions by the Site Reliability Engineer; it led to the Platform Engineer, MLOps Engineer and DevSecOps Engineer.

nodes.title: Cloud Engineer
nodes.what: Designs, provisions and operates systems on public cloud platforms: picking managed services, writing infrastructure templates, setting up accounts and permissions, and keeping costs and blast radius under control. Thinks in APIs rather than racks.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Virtualisation Engineer and the Infrastructure Engineer once compute was rented by the hour; it branched into the Kubernetes Engineer, FinOps Engineer / Analyst and Platform Engineer, and shaped the Cloud Network Engineer.

nodes.title: CI/CD / Automation Engineer
nodes.what: Builds and maintains continuous integration and delivery pipelines so every change is built, tested and deployed automatically. Focused on speed and trustworthiness of the pipeline itself: flaky tests, slow builds, caching and safe rollout steps.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Build & Release Engineer as nightly builds gave way to building every commit, with influence from the Test Automation Engineer, whose suites the pipelines run.

nodes.title: Chaos Engineer
nodes.what: Deliberately injects failures into running systems, such as killing instances, adding latency or cutting off dependencies, to prove they survive. Designs experiments with a hypothesis and a controlled blast radius rather than simply breaking things.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Site Reliability Engineer as a proactive way to test resilience, turning the lessons of past outages into planned experiments instead of waiting for the next one.

nodes.title: Kubernetes Engineer
nodes.what: Runs container orchestration clusters: upgrading control planes, tuning scheduling and autoscaling, managing networking and storage plugins, and helping teams package their services to run there. A specialist in one sprawling, fast-moving ecosystem.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Cloud Engineer as container orchestration became complex enough to need its own specialists, and much of that work was then absorbed into the Platform Engineer.

nodes.title: Platform Engineer
nodes.what: Builds an internal developer platform: paved paths, self-service templates and shared tooling that let product teams deploy and run services without becoming infrastructure experts. Treats fellow engineers as customers and the platform as a product.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the DevOps Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer, Cloud Engineer and Kubernetes Engineer as teams tired of every squad reinventing infrastructure; it led to the Developer Experience Engineer and influenced the Platform Product Manager.

nodes.title: FinOps Engineer / Analyst
nodes.what: Tracks, explains and reduces cloud spending: tagging resources, allocating costs to teams, buying commitments and flagging idle or oversized infrastructure. Sits between engineering and finance, translating usage graphs into budgets and back again.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Cloud Engineer once pay-per-use bills became large and unpredictable enough that someone had to own the money as well as the machines.

nodes.title: MLOps Engineer
nodes.what: Puts machine learning models into production and keeps them there: training pipelines, model registries, feature stores, serving infrastructure and monitoring for drift. Handles the extra moving part ordinary software lacks, the data the model learned from.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the DevOps Engineer and the Machine Learning Engineer as companies found that training a model was the easy part and running it reliably was not.

nodes.title: Observability Engineer
nodes.what: Builds the telemetry that lets engineers understand a running system: metrics, logs, traces, dashboards and alerting that fires on real problems. Aims to answer questions nobody thought to ask in advance, not just watch fixed health checks.
nodes.roots: Grew out of the Site Reliability Engineer as distributed systems made traditional monitoring insufficient and instrumentation became a specialty in its own right.

nodes.title: Software Tester
nodes.what: Runs software through planned and exploratory checks, records what fails and how to reproduce it, and reports back to the developers. The first line of defense before users find the bugs.
nodes.roots: Emerged under the influence of the Programmer as software grew too large for its authors to check alone, and led on to the QA Engineer.

nodes.title: QA Engineer
nodes.what: Owns quality across a product: writes test plans, defines acceptance criteria, tracks defects and pushes for processes that prevent bugs rather than just catching them late.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Tester as quality became a managed discipline with standards and process, and led on to the SDET.

nodes.title: SDET (Software Dev Engineer in Test)
nodes.what: A developer whose product is test code: builds harnesses, frameworks and automated suites that exercise the software, and works as a peer of the engineers whose code is being tested.
nodes.roots: Grew out of QA Engineer as testing large, fast-moving products demanded real programming skill, and led on to the Test Automation Engineer.

nodes.title: Test Automation Engineer
nodes.what: Writes and maintains automated tests and the tooling around them, wiring them into builds so every change is checked within minutes, and hunts flaky tests that erode trust in the suite.
nodes.roots: Grew out of SDET as automation became the default way to test, and in turn influenced the CI/CD / Automation Engineer role.

nodes.title: Computer (a person)
nodes.what: A person, often working in a room full of others, who carried out long chains of arithmetic by hand or desk calculator, following set procedures to produce tables, trajectories and survey results.
nodes.roots: A root of the whole tree: when electronic machines took over the arithmetic, many of these skilled calculators moved into the new work of the Programmer.

nodes.title: Coder
nodes.what: Translated a mathematician's worked-out plan into the numeric instructions an early machine could accept, then punched, checked and fed them in. The thinking was done upstream; the coder made it machine-readable without errors.
nodes.roots: A root title: the split between planning a problem and coding it collapsed as machines grew, and the job merged upward into the Programmer.

nodes.title: Programmer / Computer Programmer
nodes.what: Writes the step-by-step instructions that make a computer do a job, from working out the logic to debugging the result. The general-purpose title that most later specialties are carved out of.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Computer (a person) and Coder once one role owned both the logic and the instructions, and went on to spawn systems, application, analyst and engineering variants.

nodes.title: Systems Programmer
nodes.what: Works below the applications, on operating systems, compilers, utilities and the glue that keeps a machine running for everyone else. Cares about memory, performance and hardware quirks more than business rules.
nodes.roots: Split from Programmer as operating systems grew big enough to need dedicated staff, and later seeded the Database Administrator (DBA) and Systems Administrator roles.

nodes.title: Application Programmer
nodes.what: Builds the programs the business actually uses, such as payroll, billing and inventory, on top of the platform the systems people maintain. Success is measured in correct reports and on-time batch runs.
nodes.roots: Split from Programmer to separate business-facing code from systems code, and later folded into the broader Software Developer title.

nodes.title: Analyst/Programmer
nodes.what: Does both halves of a project: talks to users to pin down what a system should do, then writes the code. Common in smaller shops that could not afford a separate analyst and programmer.
nodes.roots: Combines Systems Analyst and Programmer into one person, and fed directly into the Software Developer title that later absorbed it.

nodes.title: Software Engineer
nodes.what: Treats building software as engineering: designing for scale and change, reviewing code, testing, and thinking about the system's whole life, not just getting one program to run.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Programmer as projects got too large to handle informally; trades ideas both ways with Software Developer and launched the senior ladder, embedded, architecture, reliability and AI roles.

nodes.title: Embedded Software Engineer
nodes.what: Writes the firmware inside devices such as cars, appliances, medical kit and routers, usually in tight memory, with real-time deadlines and direct control of hardware pins and sensors.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Engineer as cheap microprocessors put code into everyday products that demanded engineering rigor at the hardware boundary.

nodes.title: Software Developer
nodes.what: Designs, writes, tests and maintains software of almost any kind. In practice the title overlaps heavily with Software Engineer and is the everyday name for the job in many companies.
nodes.roots: Grew from Application Programmer and Analyst/Programmer as those roles merged, with a two-way influence from Software Engineer; it later branched into game, web and mobile work.

nodes.title: Game Developer
nodes.what: Builds interactive games, juggling graphics, physics, input, sound and frame-rate budgets while working alongside artists and designers. Fun and responsiveness are the spec.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Developer once home computers and consoles created a market big enough for specialists in entertainment software.

nodes.title: Webmaster
nodes.what: Ran a website more or less single-handed: wrote the pages, kept the server up, answered the contact email and fixed broken links. A generalist for a medium that was still new.
nodes.roots: A root of the web line: as sites grew complex the catch-all role faded and its building work passed to the Web Developer.

nodes.title: Web Developer
nodes.what: Builds websites and web applications, covering the markup and scripts users see and the server code and databases behind them, and ships changes far faster than boxed software ever did.
nodes.roots: Grew from Software Developer and Webmaster as websites turned into real applications that needed professional programming.

nodes.title: Front-end Developer
nodes.what: Focuses on everything that runs in the browser: layout, styling, interaction, accessibility and the client-side frameworks that tie them together. Works closely with designers.
nodes.roots: Split from Web Developer once browser-side code became rich and complicated enough to be a full-time specialty.

nodes.title: Back-end Developer
nodes.what: Builds the server side of applications: APIs, business logic, data storage, authentication and performance under load. Users never see the work directly, only its speed and correctness.
nodes.roots: Split from Web Developer as server systems grew large, distributed and data-heavy enough to need dedicated engineers.

nodes.title: Full-stack Developer
nodes.what: Works across the whole application, from browser interface to server and database, often shipping features end to end. Valued in startups and small teams for breadth over deep specialization.
nodes.roots: Recombines Front-end Developer and Back-end Developer, as modern frameworks and smaller teams made one person covering both layers practical again.

nodes.title: Mobile / iOS / Android Developer
nodes.what: Builds apps for phones and tablets, dealing with small screens, touch, battery, intermittent networks and the review rules of the app stores that distribute the software.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Developer when app stores turned smartphones into a major software platform with its own tools and conventions.

nodes.title: Senior Software Engineer
nodes.what: An experienced engineer who owns larger features with little supervision, makes sound design calls, reviews others' code and mentors juniors, while still writing much of the code.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Software Engineer as companies formalized levels to reward experience without forcing people into management, and leads on to Staff Software Engineer.

nodes.title: Principal Engineer
nodes.what: Shapes architecture and engineering strategy for a large organization, often working with executives on long-range bets and being the person called in on the hardest technical calls.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Staff Software Engineer as the next rung of the individual-contributor ladder, and leads on to Distinguished Engineer / Fellow.

nodes.title: Staff Software Engineer
nodes.what: Sets technical direction across several teams: drives cross-cutting designs, untangles hard problems, and raises the bar on others' work. Influence matters more than individual output.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Senior Software Engineer as tech companies built a parallel ladder to management, and leads on to Principal Engineer.

nodes.title: Distinguished Engineer / Fellow
nodes.what: One of a company's very top technical people, recognized for work with industry-wide impact. Usually has wide freedom to choose problems and represents the firm's technical reputation outside it.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Principal Engineer as the summit of the technical ladder, a long-established honor that spread widely once many firms adopted engineering levels.

nodes.title: Developer Experience Engineer
nodes.what: Makes other developers productive by smoothing tools, docs, SDKs, local setup and build times, treating fellow engineers as customers and measuring friction in their daily workflow.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Platform Engineer, with strong influence from Developer Advocate / DevRel, as companies recognized that developer friction was a cost worth a dedicated role.

nodes.title: Customer / Field Engineer
nodes.what: Installed, maintained and repaired computing equipment at the customer's site, often visiting regularly for preventive maintenance. Field engineers needed deep hardware knowledge and the calm to fix things with the customer watching.
nodes.roots: A root of the family; servicing machines on site seeded both the Technical Support line and the pre-sales Systems Engineer (pre-sales) line.

nodes.title: Technical Writer
nodes.what: Writes manuals, guides, reference documentation and help content so users and developers can understand a product. Good technical writers interview engineers, test the software themselves and turn tacit knowledge into clear steps.
nodes.roots: Influenced by Programmer / Computer Programmer, as software grew complex enough that explaining it became a dedicated job rather than an afterthought for coders.

nodes.title: Systems Engineer (pre-sales)
nodes.what: Works alongside sales representatives to understand a prospect's needs, design a technical fit and demonstrate that the system will work. The role wins trust with technical buyers before a contract is signed.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Customer / Field Engineer, moving technical expertise earlier in the sale; it later grew into Sales Engineer and IT Consultant.

nodes.title: Technical Support
nodes.what: Diagnoses and resolves technical problems reported by customers or staff, by phone, email or remotely. It is the front line for figuring out whether a fault is user error, configuration or a genuine defect.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Customer / Field Engineer as more problems could be solved remotely; it then grew into Help Desk Technician and Application Support Analyst.

nodes.title: IT Consultant
nodes.what: Advises organizations on technology choices, projects and implementations, usually as an outside expert billed by the day or engagement. Work ranges from strategy reviews to rolling up sleeves on a system rollout.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Systems Engineer (pre-sales) as technical advice became something sold on its own rather than bundled with hardware; it later influenced the Forward Deployed Engineer.

nodes.title: Help Desk Technician
nodes.what: Answers first-line calls and tickets from users about passwords, printers, PCs and common software, fixing what they can quickly and escalating the rest. The job demands patience and broad, practical troubleshooting.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Technical Support as personal computers put a machine on every desk and someone had to field the resulting flood of everyday questions.

nodes.title: Technology Evangelist
nodes.what: Persuades developers, partners and the public to adopt a platform by explaining its value, building enthusiasm and gathering early supporters. The work is part marketing, part technical credibility.
nodes.roots: A root title in this family, made famous around Apple's Macintosh launch; it later grew into Developer Advocate / DevRel.

nodes.title: Sales Engineer
nodes.what: The technical partner in a sales team, running demos, answering detailed product questions, building proofs of concept and scoping how a customer would deploy the product.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Systems Engineer (pre-sales) as the title spread beyond hardware vendors to software companies; it later grew into Solutions Engineer.

nodes.title: Application Support Analyst
nodes.what: Keeps specific business applications healthy in production, investigating errors, checking logs and data, applying fixes or workarounds and liaising with developers when a code change is needed.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Technical Support as companies came to depend on particular applications; it then grew into Support Engineer and influenced Site Reliability Engineer.

nodes.title: Service Desk Analyst
nodes.what: Handles incidents and service requests through a formal ticketing process, tracking priorities and service-level targets. Compared with a help desk, the emphasis is on defined processes, escalation paths and measured outcomes.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Help Desk Technician as ITIL-style service management reframed support as a catalog of services with agreed levels.

nodes.title: Support Engineer
nodes.what: Solves complex customer problems that need real engineering skill: reading code, reproducing bugs, analyzing logs and sometimes writing patches or tools. Support engineers are the bridge between customers and the product team.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Application Support Analyst as software vendors, especially in SaaS, needed support staff who could dig into code and infrastructure.

nodes.title: Developer Advocate / DevRel
nodes.what: Helps developers succeed with a platform through tutorials, sample code, talks and community work, then carries their feedback back to the product team. Advocacy runs in both directions.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Technology Evangelist, shifting from persuasion toward hands-on developer help; it in turn influenced Developer Experience Engineer.

nodes.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
nodes.what: A software engineer embedded with a customer, writing code on site to adapt a product to real, messy data and workflows. The FDE bridges sales, consulting and product engineering in one person.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Solutions Engineer and Software Engineer, with influence from IT Consultant, combining customer-facing work with shipping production code.

nodes.title: Solutions Engineer
nodes.what: Designs and demonstrates how a product solves a particular customer's problem, often building integrations, prototypes or proofs of concept. It is a more hands-on, build-oriented take on technical sales.
nodes.roots: Grew out of Sales Engineer, especially at software and cloud companies; it later grew into the Forward Deployed Engineer.
